newsitem.title: KENYA: Sudanese rebels say they seized northeast garrisons.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese rebels say they seized northeast garrisons.

text.p: Sudanese rebels said on Friday they seized three garrisons in the northeast of Africa's largest country and were threatening Port Sudan, a key link with the rest of the world.
The rebels also said they had repulsed a major army counter-attack near a key town in southern Sudan, inflicting heavy casualties.

Yassir Arman, spokesman for the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) in Eritrea's capital Asmara, said rebels captured garrisons at Karora town, Itairba and Shabri near the Eritrean border on Thursday.
"We are now advancing towards the town of Tokar," he said by telephone. Another SPLA spokesman in Nairobi said rebel forces were pursuing the remnants of the garrisons towards Tokar.
"The enemy suffered heavy casualties and large amounts of arms and ammunition were seized," said spokesman Sampson Kwaje.
Asked whether the aim of the new rebel campaign was to cut the main road from Khartoum to Port Sudan, the Islamist government's commercial link on the Red Sea, Arman said:
"This whole offensive in the east is threatening Port Sudan itself as well as the road to Khartoum."
Tokar is 100 km (60 miles) from the border with Eritrea and 150 km (90 miles) southeast of Port Sudan. The nearest stretch of the Khartoum-Port Sudan road is 100 km (60 miles) northwest of Tokar.
The Sudanese army said on Thursday Eritrean troops and Sudanese rebels were shelling Sudan army positions on Eritrea's border but the rebels denied any Eritrean forces were involved.
In Nairobi, SPLA spokesman Sampson Kwaje said on Friday rebels repulsed a major army counter-offensive on Wednesday 64 km (40 miles) south of the southern capital of Juba.
"Hundreds of enemy dead bodies litter the area while hundreds more were wounded and taken prisoner," he added.
A rebel spokesman said the northeast offensive was mounted by the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) rebel coalition and its forces included fighters from the SPLA and Beja Congress.
SPLA commander John Garang told Reuters in January part of rebel strategy was to cut communications between Khartoum and Port Sudan, about 670 km (420 miles) northeast of the capital.
Eritrea's embassy in Cairo denied Eritreans were fighting.

Sudanese army spokesman Lieutenant-General Mohamed al-Senoussi Ahmed said on Thursday Eritrean troops and "a group of outlaws" had been shelling army outposts in Karora and Itairba since early Wednesday.
He said the army was putting up "tough resistance".
Northern rebels of the opposition NDA opposition coalition attacked the army on the Sudanese side of the Eritrean border in January but that offensive failed to win much territory.
Rebel units farther south, led by the southern-based SPLA, captured the Sudanese towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan on the Ethiopian border in an attack coordinated with the northerners.
Sudan's government said Eritreans and Ethiopians did most of the fighting in both attacks but the two countries, despite very poor relations with Khartoum, said their troops had no role.
The campaign against the Islamist government shifted this month to the far south, where the SPLA captured the major town of Yei and began to advance towards the regional capital Juba.
Khartoum says Ugandan troops are fighting alongside rebels in the south but the Ugandan government denies this and accuses the Sudanese government of supporting rebels in northern Uganda.

The SPLA has been fighting since 1983 for greater autonomy or independence for the Christian and animist south from the Moslem and Arabised north. It and its allies say they want a popular uprising in Khartoum against the Islamist government.
